query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, the wear resistance is primarily governed by the formation of an adherent, protective oxide film during sliding. This oxide film, generated in reactive (oxygen‐containing) environments, serves as a barrier that reduces direct contact and abrasive wear on the underlying alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, compositionally homogeneous high-entropy alloy coating with little pre-existing oxide on the surface.
generation.intervention: Switch the wear test environment from an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) to an oxygen-rich atmosphere to promote controlled oxidation during wear.
generation.conditions: Standardized wear testing at fixed load and sliding velocity, moderate temperature (below levels that induce thermal degradation), and controlled test duration. The test should span oxygen partial pressures sufficient to form but not excessively thicken the oxide film.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanostructured, adherent oxide film forming on the coating surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, the reactive environment facilitates the in-situ formation of an oxide layer that adheres well to the high-entropy alloy. This film acts as a protective barrier reducing metal-to-metal contact and abrasive wear. In an inert environment, the absence of such a film results in higher wear due to direct mechanical action.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under controlled oxygen-rich conditions, the wear rate (e.g., material loss or wear track depth) will be significantly lower than in an inert atmosphere. Microscopic and compositional analyses should reveal a more continuous and stable oxide film in the oxygen-rich tests.
generation.baseline: Wear performance measured in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) where oxide film formation is minimized, leading to higher wear rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid under moderate sliding speeds, controlled temperature conditions (ensuring oxide stability without inducing thermal degradation), and oxygen partial pressures that allow formation of a protective oxide without oversaturating the surface. Extremes in these conditions (very high temperatures or oxygen levels that cause brittle oxide growth) may fall outside the valid range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thickness, composition, and mechanical integrity of the oxide film, as well as its interaction with the alloy’s microstructure, may vary with slight changes in alloy composition and test conditions. The exact quantitative reduction in wear is uncertain and may differ among different high-entropy alloy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel wear tests using the same high-entropy alloy coatings subjected to identical mechanical conditions (load, speed, duration, temperature). One set will be performed in an inert atmosphere (baseline) and the other in an oxygen-enriched atmosphere. Measure wear volume/loss and conduct surface analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS) to assess oxide film formation.
measurements: Quantitative wear track depth via profilometry
Material loss (e.g., via mass change measurements)
Surface morphology and chemical composition (using SEM, EDS)
Oxide film thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-rich tests do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in wear (i.e., similar or higher wear rates than the inert tests) and do not show evidence of a protective oxide film, the hypothesis would be falsified.
